titre: DABUS, the Machine Named Inventor on a Patent
accroche: Between 2019 and 2023, several patent offices refuse to recognize Stephen Thaler's AI as an inventor. Only one accepts, without settling the question.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 2019, the American engineer Stephen Thaler files patent applications in about a dozen countries and with two regional offices, for two objects: a food container whose walls follow a fractal geometry, easier to stack and assemble, and a device that attracts attention through a sequence of flashes designed for search and rescue operations. On each form, in the inventor box, he enters not his own name but that of DABUS, the artificial intelligence he designed and which produced these two ideas with no human intervention in the end result. Thaler presents himself only as the owner of the machine, claiming the rights by transfer from it.

## Five Offices, Four Refusals, and One Exception

The refusal comes first in the United Kingdom, where the patent office rejects the application on December 4, 2019; the Court of Appeal confirms in September 2021, and the Supreme Court puts a final end to it on December 20, 2023, ruling unanimously that Section 13(2)(a) of the Patents Act 1977 requires an inventor to be a natural person.

The European Patent Office follows the same path: its Legal Board of Appeal rejects Thaler's appeal on December 21, 2021, holding that an inventor designated in an application must be a person with legal capacity, which a machine, however sophisticated, does not have.

In the United States, the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit rules on August 5, 2022 in *Thaler v. Vidal*: the Patent Act reserves the word “individual” for a human being, which the court says is confirmed by the use of the pronouns “himself” and “herself” in the statute and by the obligation on every inventor to take an oath, an act that nothing shows a machine is capable of.

Australia offers a moment of uncertainty. On July 30, 2021, Justice Beach of the Federal Court finds that nothing in the Patents Act 1990 expressly rules out an artificial intelligence being an inventor. The decision makes a great stir, but the Full Court of the same court overturns it on April 13, 2022, ruling unanimously that the entire structure of the Act, an inventor who receives rights, assigns them, takes an oath, presupposes a natural person.

That leaves South Africa, the only country where DABUS appears today as an inventor on a granted patent, accepted at the end of June 2021. But the South African office (CIPC) conducts only a formal examination: it checks that the file is complete, without examining either the novelty of the invention or the validity of the person named as inventor, those questions being left, in that system, to a possible later lawsuit. The office therefore never ruled that DABUS could legally invent; it simply never had to ask itself the question.

## Four Different Laws, One Line

A British court speaks of a natural person, an American court of an individual in the ordinary sense of the term, the European Patent Office of legal capacity, the Australian court of the entire structure of its statute: texts drafted decades and oceans apart arrive at the same requirement without citing one another. The only country where DABUS won its case did not win it by settling the question, but by never asking it.

citation.texte: Congress has determined that only a natural person can be an inventor, so AI cannot be.
citation.auteur: United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit

carte.punch: Only one country let an AI become an inventor, and not for the reason you think.
carte.idee: Between 2019 and 2023, the United Kingdom, the European Patent Office, the United States and Australia on appeal all refused to recognize the AI DABUS as an inventor. Only South Africa accepted it, but its office checks only the form of applications, never who can legally invent.

quiz.question: Why does the patent granted by the South African office not prove that the country recognizes artificial intelligence as an inventor?
choix: That office does not examine the substance of applications: it only checks that the file is complete
The patent was annulled upon issue at the request of the South African government
South Africa is party to no international patent treaty, which makes the patent ineffective
DABUS was in fact named only as a co-inventor, alongside Stephen Thaler
quiz.explication: The South African system (CIPC) conducts only a formal check: it verifies that the file is complete, without examining novelty, inventive step, or who can legally be an inventor. The offices that examine the substance, in the United Kingdom, the United States, the European Patent Office and Australia on appeal, all refused DABUS.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what basis did the American Federal Circuit refuse to recognize DABUS as an inventor, in Thaler v. Vidal?
choix: The word “individual” in the Patent Act refers exclusively to a natural person
DABUS had produced no patentable invention within the meaning of the law
Thaler had not paid the filing fees required by the American office
The patent had already been refused once before for a formal defect
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The court relies on the word “individual,” which it holds is reserved for a human being, confirmed by the pronouns “himself” and “herself” in the text and the obligation to take an oath, which nothing shows a machine is capable of.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did Justice Beach of the Australian Federal Court first rule on DABUS, in July 2021?
choix: Australian law required a review by Parliament before any decision
The patent had to be suspended until the British decision
Nothing in Australian law expressly rules out an AI being an inventor
An AI could file a patent but never collect the rights
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Justice Beach finds that nothing expressly rules out an AI being an inventor under the Patents Act 1990, a decision later overturned unanimously by the Full Court in April 2022.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did the United Kingdom Supreme Court reject Thaler's application on December 20, 2023?
choix: The invention described was not judged sufficiently new by the examiners
The United Kingdom had already refused every application involving artificial intelligence
Thaler had not shown that DABUS had actually produced the two objects
Section 13(2)(a) of the Patents Act 1977 requires an inventor to be a natural person
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The unanimous judgment rests on Section 13(2)(a) of the Patents Act 1977, which requires an inventor to be a natural person, not on the novelty of the invention.
